title: Salman Rushdie's Attacker Convicted of Federal Terrorism Charges, Faces Life in Prison
excerpt: A jury needed just two hours to find Hadi Matar guilty of supporting Hezbollah and engaging in transnational terrorism over the 2022 stabbing of the Indian-born author.
body:
• Hadi Matar, 28, was convicted on all federal terrorism charges, including providing material support to Hezbollah and engaging in transnational terrorism
  • The jury in Buffalo, New York deliberated for just two hours before returning a unanimous guilty verdict on Wednesday
  • Matar, already serving 25 years for attempted murder, now faces a maximum sentence of life in prison with sentencing scheduled for November 3
  • The Indian-born British-American author Salman Rushdie, 79, was stabbed 15 times in 2022, losing sight in his right eye

A Swift Verdict

The man who stabbed author Salman Rushdie on stage at a New York literary festival in 2022 was found guilty on Wednesday of federal terrorism charges, bringing a definitive legal conclusion to one of the most shocking attacks on artistic freedom in recent memory.

https://x.com/htTweets/status/2082684266056696292

Hadi Matar, 28, a US citizen from Fairview, New Jersey, was convicted of attempting to provide material support to Lebanon's Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah, engaging in an act of transnational terrorism, and providing material support to terrorists. The jury at a US District Court in Buffalo, New York, deliberated for barely two hours before returning its unanimous verdict, according to federal prosecutors.

The Attack and Its Origins

On August 12, 2022, Matar rushed the stage at the Chautauqua Institution in Mayville, New York, where Rushdie was preparing to speak about writers' safety. He stabbed the celebrated author 15 times in the head, neck, torso, and left hand.

Rushdie, now 79, was airlifted to hospital and underwent emergency surgery. He lost sight in his right eye and suffered severe damage to internal organs. His recovery took months, and he has since written a memoir, Knife, about the attack and its aftermath.

Prosecutors presented evidence showing that Matar spent more than a year researching the fatwa — the 1989 religious edict by Iran's then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini — which called for Rushdie's death over his novel The Satanic Verses. The book was denounced as blasphemous by Khomeini, and the fatwa has never been formally rescinded.

"The Indian-born British and American novelist was preparing to speak about writers' safety when Matar stormed the stage and launched his frenzied attack."

— The Sun

From Attempted Murder to Terrorism

Matar was first convicted of attempted murder in New York state court in 2025 and sentenced to 25 years in prison. The federal terrorism charges, brought separately, carry a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. Sentencing is scheduled for November 3.

His defence team had argued that prosecutors could not prove Matar's state of mind during the attack. But the prosecution built a detailed case linking Matar's actions to the Hezbollah-supported fatwa, presenting digital evidence of his year-long research into Khomeini's edict.

A Story That Resonates With the Diaspora

Rushdie, born in Mumbai in 1947 to a Kashmiri Muslim family, is one of the most prominent literary figures of Indian origin. His work — particularly Midnight's Children, which won the Booker Prize — is deeply intertwined with the Indian subcontinent's post-independence identity. The Satanic Verses itself drew on Islamic history and immigrant experience in ways that remain both celebrated and controversial.

The conviction marks a significant moment in the long arc of the Rushdie affair, which has shaped global debates about blasphemy, free expression, and the reach of state-sponsored religious edicts for nearly four decades. For the Indian diaspora, it is a reminder that the consequences of those debates remain violently real.
